records.title: Birth
records.shortDescription: Born in Warsaw to Szmul Moszek Kaper and Maria Mucha, in a Jewish family registered in the city’s non-Christian civil records.
records.longDescription: Born on January 23 (February 5, New Style) in Warsaw. Father – Szmul Moszek (later Stanisław/Samuel) Kaper, bookkeeper, aged 28. Mother – Maria (Mariam) née Mucha, aged 24. The family is of Jewish faith (registered at the Office of Civil Status for Non-Christian Confessions, 8th Jerusalem District, Warsaw).

records.title: Transfer to the Staszic Real School
records.shortDescription: On 1 September 1915, aged thirteen, Kaper moved from Skrynnikov’s private school to the fifth class of the Staszic Real School in Warsaw.
records.longDescription: Kaper attended the private school of Aleksander M. Skrynnikov at 49 Żurawia Street, whose curriculum favoured mathematics, the sciences and modern languages over the classical programme of Latin and Greek. On 1 September 1915, aged thirteen, he transferred to the fifth class of the Stanisław Staszic Real School, which became a state gymnasium in 1918 and where he completed his secondary education.

hero.title: A. M. Skrynnikowa’s school building — examination notice, 1914
hero.altText: Clipping from a 1914 Warsaw newspaper in which the acting director of the Warsaw Seventh Boys’ Gymnasium announces examinations in the building of A. M. Skrynnikowa’s real school at Żórawia 49.
hero.rightsNote: Public-domain newspaper notice published in 1914. The local image is a cropped faithful reproduction from the CRISPA digital copy held by Biblioteka Uniwersytecka w Warszawie.

records.title: High school graduation
records.shortDescription: Kaper graduates from Warsaw’s Staszic Gymnasium and receives his matura certificate.
records.longDescription: Graduates from the Staszic Gymnasium in Warsaw and receives his diploma (matura certificate).

hero.title: Bronisław Kaper — portrait as a young man
hero.altText: Portrait of Bronisław Kaper as a young man.

records.title: University admission delayed by a disciplinary sanction
records.shortDescription: Kaper’s admission to the Faculty of Law at the University of Warsaw was delayed by a one-semester disciplinary sanction before his formal matriculation in February 1920.
records.longDescription: University records show that Kaper applied to the Faculty of Law at the University of Warsaw in October 1919, but that the Matriculation Commission rejected his immediate admission after a disciplinary incident. The sanction was temporary: he later described it in his curriculum vitae as a one-semester relegation, and he was formally entered in the faculty album on 6 February 1920.

hero.title: University of Warsaw, Kazimierzowski Palace — campus context image
hero.altText: Historical view of the Kazimierzowski Palace at the University of Warsaw.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain: archival image from Narodowe Archiwum Cyfrowe / Szukaj w Archiwach. Reproduced with attribution to NAC / Szukaj w Archiwach.

records.title: Formal matriculation at the University of Warsaw
records.shortDescription: After the one-semester delay documented separately, Kaper was formally entered in the Faculty of Law album at the University of Warsaw.
records.longDescription: This event now records the formal matriculation rather than the earlier October 1919 application. Kaper was entered in the Faculty of Law and Political Sciences album on 6 February 1920, under album number 6854.

hero.title: Bronisław Kaper’s University of Warsaw student record book — opening folios, 1920
hero.altText: Open student record book with a portrait of young Bronisław Kaper and University of Warsaw matriculation details.
hero.rightsNote: Reproduced by permission of the University of Warsaw Archives.

records.title: Police certificate records Mosaic religion
records.shortDescription: A police certificate issued shortly before Kaper’s baptism recorded his religion as “Mosaic,” the official term then used for the Jewish faith.
records.longDescription: The certificate of good conduct issued by the Warsaw State Police forms an important documentary link between Kaper’s university records and the later baptismal entry. It anchors the discussion of identity in administrative sources rather than retrospectively imposed narratives: Kaper appears in the record as a young Warsaw student from an assimilated Jewish family whose formal confessional status changed only a few months later.

records.title: Baptism
records.shortDescription: Kaper is baptized at St. Alexander’s parish in Warsaw, marking his conversion to Catholicism.
records.longDescription: On July 17, Kaper is baptized at the Roman Catholic Parish of St. Alexander in Warsaw, at the age of 18. The baptism marks his conversion from Judaism to Catholicism.

hero.title: St. Alexander’s Church, Warsaw — context photograph, 1939
hero.altText: St. Alexander’s Church on Three Crosses Square in Warsaw, visible in a 1939 photograph of a 3 May parade.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain: interwar archival photograph held by Szukaj w Archiwach. Credit Szukaj w Archiwach, “Uroczystości święta 3 Maja w Warszawie,” sygn. 3/1/0/6/2877/33.

records.title: War
records.shortDescription: Kaper serves as a volunteer in the Polish–Soviet War before returning to university life.
records.longDescription: Serves as a volunteer in the Polish-Soviet War in the rank of Senior Private (starszy szeregowy) in the Reserve Depot (Skadrowany Zapasowy) of the 1st Reconnaissance Aviation Regiment (1. Pułk Lotniczy Wywiadowczy), stationed at Mokotów, Warsaw. On November 5, he is granted indefinite leave as an “academic volunteer” (akademik ochotnik), allowing him to resume his university studies.

hero.title: Wstąp do wojska broń Ojczyzny! — 1920
hero.altText: Printed Polish appeal of 1920 calling men to join the army and defend the country.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain: ephemera held by Archiwum Państwowe w Lublinie, digitised in Szukaj w Archiwach. Reproduced with attribution to Archiwum Państwowe w Lublinie.

records.title: Music studies at the Chopin Music School in Warsaw
records.shortDescription: Kaper studies piano and composition in Warsaw while building a strong theoretical musical foundation.
records.longDescription: His training covered piano, theory, harmony, counterpoint, composition, form and orchestration, and most probably combined piano study with the history and aesthetics of music.

hero.title: Warsaw Philharmonic at Jasna and Sienkiewicza streets — published 1933
hero.altText: Sepia street view of the Warsaw Philharmonic building at the corner of Jasna and Henryka Sienkiewicza streets, with pedestrians in the foreground.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain as marked by Biblioteka Narodowa / Polona. Cropped from p. 4 of the 1933 publication; photographer not identified.

records.title: Earliest dated compositions
records.shortDescription: Two manuscripts of 1923 are the earliest dated compositions in the Kaper Papers: Rozmowa, a concert song for voice and piano, and Koszutski Girls, written for the revue stage.
records.longDescription: The American Heritage Center holds two Kaper manuscripts dated 1923: Rozmowa (Conversation), a concert song for voice and piano, and Koszutski Girls, a piece for voice and piano belonging to the world of the Warsaw revue, whose first page of music is already signed “Mus. B. Asper”. Neither carries a month, so no order can be established between them, and neither can be called the first thing Kaper wrote: they are the earliest pieces that survive with a date. Earlier accounts single out Rozmowa as his first serious composition; that judgement belongs to those accounts, not to the manuscripts.

records.title: Koszutski Girls and the B. Asper pseudonym
records.shortDescription: The manuscript Koszutski Girls shows Kaper already working with revue-dance conventions and using the B. Asper signature that would later appear in printed songs.
records.longDescription: Koszutski Girls complicates a simple division between Kaper’s concert training and his later popular-song career. Although preserved as an autograph manuscript, the piece is tied to Warsaw revue culture and to the international fashion for “girls” troupes. Its practical performance marking and the signature “Mus. B. Asper” foreshadow the pseudonymous popular-song activity of 1926–1927, making it a useful early marker of Kaper’s movement between concert idiom, cabaret practice, and commercial entertainment.

hero.title: Koszutski Girls in Teatr “Perskie Oko”: przegląd rewji (1926)
hero.altText: Illustrated theatre-programme page with portraits and three group photographs labeled Koszutski-Girls.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain according to the Mazowiecka Biblioteka Cyfrowa catalog record; unrestricted public access.

records.title: Application to Faculty of Philosophy
records.shortDescription: Kaper seeks to transfer from law to the humanities, while taking academic leave.
records.longDescription: In September, applies for transfer to the Faculty of Philosophy, Humanities Section. The immatriculation committee conditionally accepts him, pending a certificate of departure from the Faculty of Law. Takes academic leave for the winter and summer semesters of 1923/24.

records.title: Official completion of law studies
records.shortDescription: Kaper completes his law studies, passing the final exam and receiving formal university documents.
records.longDescription: Kaper passed the three prescribed faculty examinations in sequence: the legal-historical on 5 April 1922 with the grade good, the political on 30 April 1923 and the judicial on 14 February 1925, both satisfactory. He received his Certificate of Departure (Świadectwo Wystąpienia) no. 944 on 26 May, and the Faculty of Law diploma no. 924 is dated 13 June 1925.

hero.title: University of Warsaw Gate — law-studies context image
hero.altText: Historical view of the entrance gate to the University of Warsaw.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain according to the Szukaj w Archiwach / NAC source page recorded for this image. Use with attribution to Narodowe Archiwum Cyfrowe / Szukaj w Archiwach. This is a contextual image, not evidence of Kaper’s physical presence in the depicted scene.

records.title: Public performance at the Chopin Music School concert
records.shortDescription: Kaper performs Chopin in a public concert as a pupil of Józef Śmidowicz’s piano class.
records.longDescription: In June, appears at a public concert of the Fryderyk Chopin Higher School of Music at the Warsaw Philharmonic as a pupil of Józef Śmidowicz’s piano class. Performs the first movement of Chopin’s Piano Concerto in F minor. Warsaw critics note his “light finger technique” and “elegance combined with concentrated lyricism,”

hero.title: Nasz Przegląd, 1925 — Chopin Music School recital notice
hero.altText: Polish newspaper clipping from Nasz Przegląd, 1925.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain: anonymous press notice, 1925. Anonymous works are PD 70 years after publication (expired); also PD in the US (published before 1929).

records.title: Entry into Warsaw popular song: Craig, Włast, and Altschuler
records.shortDescription: Kaper later traced his entry into popular song to a Warsaw network linking “Henry Craig,” Andrzej Włast, cabaret performance, and Altschuler’s publishing house.
records.longDescription: Kaper’s own account presents the move into songwriting as accidental: a friend whom he called “Henry Craig” introduced him to a leading Warsaw lyricist identifiable as Andrzej Włast, after which the song reached the cabaret stage and then print. Read together with the surviving printed songs, this episode explains how a composer trained in concert idioms entered the commercial structures of interwar Warsaw popular song: lyricist, cabaret performer, publisher, and sheet-music circulation.
records.searchPeople: Andrzej Włast Bronisław Kaper Henryk Gold

hero.title: A zresztą niech pan do mnie zadzwoni... — sheet music, Polona
hero.altText: Sheet music cover for “A zresztą niech pan do mnie zadzwoni...,” with printed credits for Willy and Br. Asper.

records.title: Earliest published cabaret songs
records.shortDescription: Kaper’s Warsaw cabaret songs appear in print under the pseudonym Bruno Asper, which the manuscripts show him already using in 1923.
records.longDescription: Songs for Warsaw cabarets published under the pseudonym Bruno Asper, to words by Andrzej Włast. The printed editions of 1926 are the earliest published songs documented here; the signature itself is older, appearing on the 1923 manuscript of Koszutski Girls.

hero.title: Zula Pogorzelska in My chcemy króla at Teatr Perskie Oko (1926)
hero.altText: Black-and-white stage photograph of Zula Pogorzelska posing with a folding fan in an ornate costume and large decorative hat.
hero.rightsNote: The linked source identifies this item as public domain or otherwise free of known copyright restrictions; attribution is retained.

records.title: Move to Berlin
records.shortDescription: Kaper leaves Warsaw for Berlin to continue his musical education and professional development.
records.longDescription: Leaves Warsaw for Berlin to continue music education.

hero.title: Berlin, Potsdamer Platz with Columbushaus — context photograph, 1933
hero.altText: Black-and-white street view of Berlin’s Potsdamer Platz with the Columbushaus building.
hero.rightsNote: Public-domain route via Wikimedia Commons. The Commons file identifies Waldemar Titzenthaler as author and marks the image as public domain / Public Domain Mark 1.0; Titzenthaler died in 1937. Use as a Berlin Potsdamer Platz / Columbushaus context image.

records.title: Earliest documented collaboration with Fritz Rotter
records.shortDescription: A 1926 manuscript of Hätt’ ich einen Kammerdiener documents an early collaboration between Kaper and Fritz Rotter, before sound film became his main professional platform.
records.longDescription: The manuscript credit for Hätt’ ich einen Kammerdiener places Kaper beside Fritz Rotter at an early point in his Berlin years. It is an important transitional event: Rotter linked Kaper to the practical economy of the German hit song—publishers, performers, promotion, and sheet-music circulation—before those skills were absorbed into the machinery of early sound film. It also explains why Rotter later became the mediator who brought Kaper and Walter Jurmann together.
records.searchPeople: Bronisław Kaper Fritz Rotter Walter Jurmann

hero.altText: Portrait of the lyricist Fritz Rotter.
hero.rightsNote: The linked source identifies this item as public domain or otherwise free of known copyright restrictions; attribution is retained.

records.title: Private study and first Berlin networks
records.shortDescription: Kaper builds his Berlin career through private study with Moritz Mayer-Mahr and Walther Gmeindl, early publications, and collaboration with Fritz Rotter.
records.longDescription: After moving to Berlin, Kaper developed his professional position through private study with pianist Moritz Mayer-Mahr and composer-conductor Walther Gmeindl, while also entering the German-language song market through Fritz Rotter and early publications under the title “Dr. Kaper.” By his own account in the 1975 oral-history interview, it was the composer Jerzy Fitelberg, among the friends he found in Berlin, who urged him to study privately rather than at the Hochschule. He had come to Berlin intending to enrol at the Staatliche Akademische Hochschule für Musik, but gave up the idea of a virtuoso career before the entrance examination, and a plan to study privately with Artur Schnabel foundered on the fees. Róża Etkin, whom he knew from the Chopin school in Warsaw, sent him to Mayer-Mahr, who urged him not to abandon the piano.
records.searchPeople: Bronisław Kaper Fritz Rotter Moritz Mayer-Mahr Walther Gmeindl Jerzy Fitelberg

records.title: Marriage
records.shortDescription: Kaper marries Eleonora Sirot in Berlin.
records.longDescription: Kaper marries Eleonora de domo Sirot in Berlin on June 30.

hero.title: Marriage register, Standesamt I in Berlin — archival document, Kaper entry, 1927
hero.altText: Cropped row from a Standesamt I register naming Bronisław Kaper.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain: official marriage-register record, 1927 (Landesarchiv Berlin).

records.title: First performance of a work by Kaper at the Bach-Saal
records.shortDescription: Róża Etkin gives the first performance of a work by B. Kaper in her recital at the Bach-Saal in Berlin.
records.longDescription: Róża Etkin had already played works by Kaper in Berlin in the spring of 1927: Signale für die musikalische Welt (no. 20) reviewed a recital devoted partly to Chopin and partly to newer Polish composers, naming Szymanowski and B. Kaper but not his works. On 3 December 1927 she gave a recital at the Bach-Saal whose programme — four Chopin ballades and works by Karol Szymanowski, Maurice Ravel and Isaac Albéniz, with Liszt’s Sonata in B minor — included the first performance of a work by B. Kaper. The announcement does not name the work. Kaper later recalled writing a piano sonatina for Etkin, which she played in Berlin; the Sonatina manuscript is dated 1927, but no source ties it to either recital.

hero.title: Blüthner-Saal entrance, Lützowstraße 76, Berlin, 1912
hero.altText: Black-and-white photograph of the ornate façade of Lützowstraße 76 in Berlin, with the entrance to the Blüthner-Saal and signs for Blüthner pianos and Oskar Schwalm’s Piano-Magazin, printed above a short advertising notice.
hero.rightsNote: Public-domain historical photograph: the printed image is dated to 1912 and no photographer is identified. The local file is a faithful, reduced-size reproduction used to document the venue.

records.title: Jazz Piano Partnership
records.shortDescription: Kaper records jazz-influenced piano-duo arrangements with Hermann Biek, credited on the recordings as Hermann Bick, for Polydor.
records.longDescription: Together with the pianist Hermann Biek, credited on records as Hermann Bick, Kaper recorded six two-piano arrangements for Deutsche Grammophon/Polydor in 1928: “The Varsity Drag”, “The Song Is Ended”, “Miss Annabelle Lee”, “Ice-Cream”, “My Inspiration” and “My Pet”. In the same year Das Theater listed Kaper at the Kabarett der Komiker performing “Jazz auf zwei Klavieren” in a duo with the pianist Sula Lewitsch.

hero.title: Polydor 10237-B — “Song Is Ended,” Hermann Bick and Dr. Kaper
hero.altText: Black-and-gold Polydor record label for “Song Is Ended,” crediting Hermann Bick and Dr. Kaper on two pianos; catalogue 10237-B.
hero.rightsNote: The YouTube upload documents the historical Polydor label but supplies no reusable licence for the video frame, and the photographer or scanner of the disc is not identified. Rights in the modern frame capture and in the historical label cannot be established from the supplied metadata, so the image remains copyright undetermined.

records.title: Performance of piano pieces
records.shortDescription: Eliza Rozenblum performs three unidentified piano pieces by Kaper at the Warsaw Conservatory Hall.
records.longDescription: Kurjer Warszawski of 18 January 1928 reviewed a recital at the Warsaw Conservatory Hall by Eliza Rozenblum, a pupil of Zbigniew Drzewiecki, whose programme included “three piano pieces by B. Kaper”. Felicjan Szopski found in them the promise of a young composer, while Adam Wieniawski heard impressionist models of sonority and an indeterminacy of form. The titles are not recorded, and the phrase may equally describe the three movements of the Sonatina.

hero.title: Warsaw Conservatory at 1 Okólnik Street — before 1939
hero.altText: Black-and-white historical exterior view of the Warsaw Conservatory building at 1 Okólnik Street.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain under the Wikimedia Commons PD-Poland assessment: an anonymous photograph published in Poland before 1939 without a copyright notice.

records.title: Earliest publications and recordings with Fritz Rotter
records.shortDescription: The earliest published tangos and foxtrots by Kaper and Fritz Rotter documented here appear in German and Viennese editions.
records.longDescription: Tangos and foxtrots by “Dr. Kaper” published in German and Viennese editions. Their working relationship is older than the printed songs: a manuscript of 1926 already places the two names together.

hero.title: Tot Weerziens, Mijnheer Jansen — sheet-music cover
hero.altText: Sheet-music cover for the Dutch-language edition “Tot Weerziens, Mijnheer Jansen”.
hero.rightsNote: The cover artwork is signed Hassel, but the illustrator’s identity and rights history have not been established. A reduced-resolution image is used for scholarly identification and commentary; rights in the underlying music and lyrics are separate.

records.title: Involvement in Polish cultural life in Berlin
records.shortDescription: Kaper conducts a concert of the Berlin “Harmonja” given within the Polish community.
records.longDescription: In its report on the Polish colony in Berlin, the Berlin correspondent of “Kurjer Warszawski” (27 March 1929) records that a concert of the Berlin “Harmonja,” conducted by “the young composer dr. Bronisław Kaper,” took place strictly within the Polish community, with the tenor Salecki of the Dresden Opera and the soprano Głowacka. The report covers the preceding months and gives no date for the concert; it does not describe the ensemble further. In his 1975 oral history Kaper recalled conducting “the Polish Choir” in Berlin.

hero.title: Kurjer Warszawski, 27 March 1929 — Harmonja concert conducted by Kaper
hero.altText: Newspaper paragraph in Polish reporting a concert of the Berlin “Harmonja” conducted by dr. Bronisław Kaper.
hero.rightsNote: Public domain: anonymous press notice, 1929. Anonymous works are PD 70 years after publication (expired); also PD in the US (published through 1930).

records.title: ERKLA-Quartett concert review in Hamborn
records.shortDescription: A Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung review documents Kaper’s appearance with the ERKLA four-piano ensemble in Hamborn, alongside Giuliano Pomeranz, then performing as Julian Pomeranc, Alexander Zakin, and Leopold Mittmann.
records.longDescription: Dr. Funk’s review “Jazz auf vier Flügeln” in the Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung, 10 December 1929, p. 12, documents an ERKLA concert in Hamborn. It names Kaper alongside Giuliano Pomeranz, then performing as Julian Pomeranc, Alexander Zakin, and Leopold Mittmann. Kaper joined the ensemble after Adam Gelbtrunk’s departure, at Leopold Mittmann’s urging; the announcements of the late 1920s otherwise list the quartet without him, so the association cannot be counted as a regular one. Dr. Funk credited him with a “Vierflügeltango” of sonorous linear writing and Mittmann with a “Jazz-Prélude” and three “Jazz-Babies”.

records.title: Bick & Kaper at Berlin premiere
records.shortDescription: The Bick und Kaper piano duo plays before a Berlin film premiere and attracts press attention.
records.longDescription: The Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung of 14 February 1929 reports that the evening at the Ufa-Theater Universum in Berlin, the première of Der Adjutant des Zaren with Ivan Mosjoukine and Carmen Boni, opened with the jazz piano duo Bick und Kaper, “die Jazz auf zwei Flügeln darboten”. records.title: Earliest documented compositions for film
records.shortDescription: Kaper’s earliest documented work for the cinema is music for three German sound films of 1930.
records.longDescription: Music for Die lustigen Musikanten, directed by Max Obal, Alraune, directed by Richard Oswald, and Der Korvettenkapitän, directed by Rudolf Walther-Fein, all released in 1930. For Alraune Kaper wrote two tangos to words by Fritz Rotter, “Nur Tango, nur Tango” and “Wenn mich Männer betrügen”; Der Korvettenkapitän carried four of his songs, again to Rotter’s words.

records.title: Alraune as Kaper’s first documented sound-film commission
records.shortDescription: Alraune marks Kaper’s first clearly documented entry into early sound film, through songs rather than background scoring in the later Hollywood sense.
records.longDescription: Kaper’s first documented sound-film work belongs to the early phase of cinema in which the film composer’s task was still closely tied to song production. Alraune, Richard Oswald’s 1930 sound remake, did not yet require the later Hollywood model of continuous underscoring. Instead, Kaper contributed songs that could serve the film while also entering the wider economy of printed scores, records, performers, and radio.

records.title: Meeting Walter Jurmann
records.shortDescription: Fritz Rotter pairs Kaper with Walter Jurmann in 1931, at the start of the partnership that shapes his European film career.
records.longDescription: Fritz Rotter paired the two composers in 1931, when each had already had separate successes and sound film was multiplying commissions. Their names first stand together in the credits of Die große Attraktion, directed by Max Reichmann, but three of the film’s songs were registered under Kaper’s name alone: “Du warst mir ein Roman”, the slow fox written for Richard Tauber, “Das verliebte Orchester” and “Ich steh’ im Schnee und wart’ auf dich”. The first film signed jointly throughout is Ehe mit beschränkter Haftung.

records.title: The Sängerfilm and the star-singer circuit
records.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann’s songs entered the Sängerfilm economy, where screen performance, star singers, sheet music, records, radio, and dance-band repertory reinforced one another.
records.longDescription: The Kaper–Jurmann partnership developed inside the commercial ecology of early European musical film. Their songs for productions associated with singers such as Richard Tauber and Jan Kiepura were not simply film numbers: they were designed to travel beyond the screen as printed music, recordings, radio items, and repertory for performers. This star-singer circuit explains why the duo’s European experience later appeared useful to MGM, which read it through the promotional language of Viennese musical competence.
records.searchPeople: Bronisław Kaper Walter Jurmann Jan Kiepura Richard Tauber

records.title: Multiple-language versions and transnational sound-film production
records.shortDescription: Before 1933, Kaper and Jurmann were already working within the multiple-language version system that linked Babelsberg, Joinville, Vienna, and other European production centres.
records.longDescription: The practice of producing parallel language versions was one of the key industrial conditions of early sound cinema. It allowed music to move more easily than dialogue across national markets, even when lyrics, singers, and performance contexts changed. Kaper and Jurmann’s work in this system gave their songs and professional skills a transnational character before their forced departure from Germany.

records.title: Flourishing Berlin collaboration
records.shortDescription: The Jurmann–Kaper partnership flourishes across German films and popular songs.
records.longDescription: Numerous German films with Jurmann–Kaper music, including “Hochzeitsreise zu dritt”, “Skandal in der Parkstraße”, “Es wird schon wieder besser”, and “Der glückliche Herr Fünf”, announced in 1932 and released in 1933 as “Ich will Dich Liebe lehren”.

records.title: Ufa resolves to terminate the contracts of its Jewish staff
records.shortDescription: One day after Goebbels addressed the film industry at the Hotel Kaiserhof, the Ufa board resolved to end the contracts of its Jewish staff.
records.longDescription: On 28 March 1933 Joseph Goebbels addressed representatives of the film industry at the Hotel Kaiserhof in Berlin. The next day the board of Universum-Film AG resolved in principle that contracts with its Jewish employees were to be terminated wherever possible, each board member deciding who in his department was to go at once and who was to be removed “im Wege eines langsamen Abbaues”, through a gradual reduction. The resolution was not limited to German citizens, so it reached Kaper and Jurmann as well, and its effect on their work was visible during the production of Kind, ich freu’ mich auf Dein Kommen.

records.title: “German film” redefined by citizenship and origin
records.shortDescription: An amendment tied the definition of a “German film” to the citizenship and origin of everyone working on it, closing the German market to Kaper and Jurmann.
records.longDescription: Two measures turned exclusion into law. The implementing ordinance of 1 July 1932 required that 75 per cent of a film production’s personnel be German, which already told against foreign composers without naming Jews. Its amendment of 28 June 1933 went further and redefined a “German film” by the German citizenship and origin of all those involved in the production. As Jewish citizens of Poland and Austria, Kaper and Jurmann were caught by both conditions at once, and the German market was closed to them.

records.title: Migration from Berlin via Vienna to Paris
records.shortDescription: After Nazi persecution intensifies, Kaper and Jurmann leave Berlin and relocate toward Paris.
records.longDescription: In 1933, after UFA terminated the contracts of its Jewish employees, Kaper and Jurmann left Berlin and, by way of Vienna, settled in Paris. His route ran through Vienna, where he had supervised the French version of Abenteuer am Lido, and the departure itself falls between the spring and the summer of 1933. Kaper’s oral history returns twice to an attack on him and his wife by a group of Nazis in a Berlin street, once within a story about self-defence and once as an aside to his account of film work, where he set it apart from his music. The attack does not explain his music, but it marks the point at which working conditions in the German film industry could no longer be separated from questions of safety.

records.title: Paris period
records.shortDescription: Kaper works in Paris for French producers, contributing songs and film music with Jurmann.
records.longDescription: About eighteen months of work for French producers. Matthias Brzoska describes Paris for the duo as less a place of exile than a career stage: in the 1933/34 season their revues dominated the Folies Bergère and the Casino de Paris, and they wrote for the Casino revue Parade de France. Besides French versions of earlier German films, Kaper and Jurmann supplied the music for Une femme au volant, On a volé un homme, Le Greluchon délicat and Les Nuits moscovites, with hits including “Natacha” and “On n’aime qu’une fois”. Jacques Ibert praised the Nuits moscovites score in Le Matin as never intrusive and always suited to its subject. The Paris address Kaper gave on arrival in New York was the Château Frontenac hotel at 54 rue Pierre Charron.

records.title: Songs beyond cinema
records.shortDescription: Jurmann–Kaper songs move beyond cinema into the French concert and festival repertoire.
records.longDescription: Jurmann–Kaper songs enter the French concert repertoire. At a summer festival in Montpellier, a jazz orchestra performs “Ninon, quand tu me souris” from “Tout pour l’amour” on an open-air stage.

records.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann attend a Paris reception for Jan Kiepura as composers of Tout pour l’amour.
records.longDescription: In February, Kaper attends a cocktail reception for Jan Kiepura at the George V in Paris together with Walter Jurmann. A contemporary press report names them among the invited guests and identifies them as the composers of the music for Tout pour l’amour.

records.title: Ninon reaches Louis B. Mayer: the Ritz meeting and MGM contract
records.shortDescription: The European success of Ninon reportedly brought Kaper and Jurmann to the attention of Louis B. Mayer, leading to a meeting at the Hôtel Ritz and an MGM contract.
records.longDescription: Kaper later recalled that the success of Ninon—written for Tout pour l’amour, the French version of Ein Lied für Dich—was the turning point that opened the path to Hollywood. Louis B. Mayer reached Paris on 7 August 1934, on a European trip that combined business with the search for new talent, and reportedly asked to meet the song’s authors, heard them perform at the Hôtel Ritz, and offered a seven-year MGM contract.

records.title: Arrival in New York en route to Los Angeles
records.shortDescription: Kaper arrives in New York from France with Eleonora, holding a temporary visa and travelling onward to Los Angeles.
records.longDescription: Kaper and his wife Eleonora sailed from Le Havre on 17 October 1934 aboard the S.S. Champlain in second cabin class and reached New York on 24 October. Their non-immigrant visas had been issued in Paris on 15 October, numbered in a single series with the Jurmanns’ (NI 1581–1584), and the manifest records Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer as having paid the passage and as the party they were joining in Culver City. Kaper gave his occupation as musician and declared that he meant to stay about eight months and then return, without seeking United States citizenship. David Blum of the Culver Export Corporation met them in New York, and they left for Hollywood on 27 October.

records.title: MGM markets Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”
records.shortDescription: American studio publicity recast Kaper and Jurmann as a Viennese composing team, turning “Vienna” into a promotional brand rather than a biographical fact.
records.longDescription: Soon after their arrival at MGM, the American press and studio publicity presented Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”. The label suited MGM’s first use of the duo in Escapade, a Hollywood remake of the Viennese film Maskerade, but it was biographically misleading for Kaper, whose career had developed in Warsaw and Berlin. The event marks the moment when Hollywood began to translate his European professional history into a marketable studio identity. The label outlasted their arrival: in December 1936 the Viennese paper Telegraf itself wrote of “die Wiener Komponisten Kaper und Jurmann”.

records.title: European afterlife
records.shortDescription: Jurmann–Kaper films and songs continue circulating in Europe after the composers leave for America.
records.longDescription: While the composers head to America, their European films and songs continue to circulate. In September 1934, “Madame wird kinderlieb” still plays in Stuttgart with Jurmann and Kaper credited — despite Nazi purges. In France, “Tout pour l’amour” with Kiepura screens as late as 1936; the Journal de Vichy calls their music “infiniment plaisante.”

records.title: Legal Permanent Entry
records.shortDescription: Kaper enters the United States for permanent residence through Calexico with Eleonora.
records.longDescription: Enters for permanent residence at Calexico, California, from Mexicali on 1 November 1935, travelling on foot with Eleonora. The manifest records 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood, as his U.S. destination; his Declaration of Intention four months later records the same address as his residence. The crossing followed the Immigration and Naturalization Service pre-examination procedure: Kaper gave the Commercial Hotel in Mexicali as his last permanent residence abroad and entered on a consular immigration visa, C.I.V. no. 1/24, issued there under Section 5 of the Immigration Act of 1924 and charged to the Polish quota. The manifest records his previous stay in California from 24 October 1934 to 20 October 1935, and his Polish passport no. 10568, issued by the Consulate General in Paris on 5 August 1934 and expired on 25 August 1935.

records.title: Hollywood debut
records.shortDescription: Kaper makes his Hollywood debut at MGM, contributing to Escapade and other major studio projects.
records.longDescription: The first American score documented here is “Escapade” (dir. Robert Z. Leonard) with William Powell and Luise Rainer. Press hails “Two New Composers” of Kiepura’s European hits. Songs also for Marx Brothers’ “A Night at the Opera” (with Ned Washington) and “Mutiny on the Bounty”. MGM engaged Kaper at first as a song specialist rather than as a film composer, and by his own account he moved only gradually from songwriter to composer of scores. For Escapade, which opened in July 1935, he supplied a single number, “You’re All I Need”, to words by Gus Kahn.

records.title: San Francisco success and Three Smart Girls
records.shortDescription: The title song from San Francisco becomes a major hit, while Kaper and Jurmann also contribute to Universal’s Three Smart Girls.
records.longDescription: The success of San Francisco made Kaper and Jurmann more visible in Hollywood and helped establish Kaper’s reputation beyond the MGM studio system. The event also includes Three Smart Girls, the Universal production associated with Deanna Durbin and Joseph Pasternak. Tommy Dorsey’s recording of the title song stood third in the Victor column of The Billboard’s ten best records for the week ended 3 August 1936.

records.title: Declarations of Intention
records.shortDescription: Bronisław and Eleonora Kaper file Declarations of Intention to become U.S. citizens in Los Angeles.
records.longDescription: On 4 February 1936, Bronisław Kaper and Eleonora Kaper each filed a Declaration of Intention in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, Los Angeles. Bronisław Kaper’s declaration records him as residing at Château des Fleurs, 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood. A Certificate of Arrival issued on 2 January 1936 had confirmed the Calexico entry, in a document valid, as its own form states, for naturalisation purposes only; its number, 23-46078, recurs on the declaration and ties the two documents together.

records.title: European Film Fund
records.shortDescription: Kaper participates in the European Film Fund, helping support refugees from the European film community.
records.longDescription: The European Film Fund was established in 1938 by Paul Kohner, Ernst Lubitsch, and Carl Laemmle to aid refugees arriving from Europe. Kaper participated in the Fund despite his relatively secure position at MGM. A surviving donor list for 1 May 1941–30 April 1942 records “Kaper, Bronislaw” and a contribution of $120, providing direct documentary evidence of his involvement.

records.title: End of an era
records.shortDescription: The Jurmann–Kaper collaboration ends amicably as Hollywood’s musical priorities change.
records.longDescription: Amicable end of Jurmann–Kaper collaboration; industry changes reduce demand for thematic songs.

records.title: New chapter
records.shortDescription: Kaper remains at MGM and begins a new solo chapter as a film composer.
records.longDescription: Kaper stayed at MGM after the partnership with Jurmann ended and moved, by his own account gradually, from writing songs to composing film scores.

records.title: Duke Ellington records “All God’s Chillun Got Rhythm”
records.shortDescription: Duke Ellington and His Famous Orchestra record “All God’s Chillun Got Rhythm” in New York, carrying a Kaper–Jurmann film song into the jazz repertoire.
records.longDescription: Duke Ellington and His Famous Orchestra recorded “All God’s Chillun Got Rhythm” in New York on 8 June 1937 for Master (MA 137, matrix M 519-1). Written by Bronisław Kaper and Walter Jurmann with words by Gus Kahn for A Day at the Races, the song passed from the screen into the jazz repertoire.

records.title: “You’re All I Need” among the most-played songs of 1935–36
records.shortDescription: Motion Picture Herald publishes the ASCAP tabulation of songs broadcast most often in 1935–36; “You’re All I Need” ranks 14th with 21,424 performances on NBC and CBS.
records.longDescription: On 5 September 1936 Motion Picture Herald printed the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers tabulation of the 112 songs performed at least 10,000 times over the NBC and CBS networks during 1935–36. “You’re All I Need,” written for Escapade, ranked 14th with 21,424 broadcasts — placing Kaper and Jurmann’s first American song among that year’s most-played titles, one year after their arrival. The list credits the film under its working title Lie Like Gentlemen and prints Jurmann’s name as “Walter Jarmann.”

records.title: Kaper’s name in German film credits
records.shortDescription: In 1933 Kaper’s name was struck from some German film credits and kept in others.
records.longDescription: In April 1933 the Polish daily Nowiny Codzienne reported from Berlin that German censorship had removed the name of “p. Bronisław Kaper,” a Pole from Warsaw, from the German version of Ein Lied für Dich, which had just had its premiere at the Gloria-Palast; no other source confirms this. When Ufa released Kind, ich freu’ mich auf Dein Kommen in June, neither Kaper nor Jurmann was named in the credits or the advertising, which gave the music to Hans O. Borgmann. The pattern was not uniform, however. In January 1933 the Berlin censors had banned the poster for Madame wünscht keine Kinder, judging it, together with the film’s title, liable to overexcite young viewers; the decision did not concern the music. Shown as Madame wird kinderlieb, the film was advertised in Bielefeld on 25 August 1933 with the credit “Musik von Jurmann und Kaper,” on the same page as an advertisement for Hans F. K. Günther’s Kleine Rassenkunde des deutschen Volkes, and a Stuttgart cinema notice of September 1934 still named Jurmann and Kaper as its composers.
